title: Chapter 1.  Geography — Location, the Four Enclaves & Physical Features

blocks.content: Puducherry's geography is defined by one unusual structural fact: it is not one contiguous territory but FOUR separate, non-contiguous enclaves scattered along India's south-eastern and south-western coasts, each a former French colonial possession. This chapter establishes that framework before moving into history and polity.

The Union Territory of Puducherry consists of four small, physically separate enclaves, each surrounded by a different mainland state, reflecting their shared origin as separate French colonial trading posts (comptoirs) rather than a single contiguous territory.

This four-part, non-contiguous structure makes Puducherry geographically similar in concept to DNH&DD (three enclaves) and the erstwhile Goa-Daman-Diu grouping - all former non-British European colonial holdings whose scattered, coast-hugging enclave pattern reflects the trading-post logic of early modern European commercial empires rather than territorial contiguity.

cells: Bay of Bengal (Coromandel Coast) - largest and capital region
Surrounded by Tamil Nadu (Thanjavur/Nagapattinam area), further south of Puducherry town
Arabian Sea (Malabar Coast) - the only Puducherry region on India's WEST coast
Surrounded by Andhra Pradesh (East Godavari/Konaseema area), on the Godavari delta

blocks.content: ★ EXAM POINT: Mahe is the ONLY one of Puducherry's four regions on India's WEST coast (Arabian Sea/Malabar Coast, surrounded by Kerala) - Puducherry town, Karaikal and Yanam are all on the EAST coast (Bay of Bengal, surrounded by Tamil Nadu and Andhra Pradesh respectively). This is one of the most frequently tested geography facts about the UT.

Puducherry's terrain is overwhelmingly flat coastal plain, typical of India's eastern Coromandel Coast and the Godavari delta (Yanam) and Malabar Coast (Mahe) settings - there are no significant hill ranges or mountainous terrain anywhere in the UT, distinguishing it sharply from the Himalayan and hill-terrain UTs covered elsewhere.

Puducherry town itself is bisected by a canal (the historic 'Grand Canal') separating the old 'White Town' (the former French quarter, with its grid-planned colonial streets) from the 'Black Town' (the traditional Tamil quarter) - a distinctive colonial-era urban planning legacy still visible in the town's layout today (Chapter 9).

The Bahour and Ousteri (Oussudu) wetlands near Puducherry town, and the backwater/estuarine environment of Yanam on the Godavari delta, represent the UT's most ecologically significant wetland habitats (Chapter 10).

cells: approx 490 sq km (Puducherry region approx 293 sq km; Karaikal approx 160 sq km; Mahe approx 9 sq km; Yanam approx 30 sq km)
Flat coastal plain; no significant hills or mountains
4 (one per region: Puducherry, Karaikal, Mahe, Yanam)
Hot and humid, typical of the Tamil Nadu/Coromandel Coast coastal climate
Comparatively lighter rainfall (Puducherry lies in the rain-shadow of the Western Ghats relative to the South-West monsoon)
The PRIMARY rainy season for Puducherry and the wider Tamil Nadu coast, bringing the bulk of annual rainfall

blocks.content: ★ EXAM POINT: Unlike most of India, Puducherry (like the rest of Tamil Nadu's Coromandel Coast) receives the BULK of its annual rainfall from the North-East (retreating) Monsoon (Oct-Dec), not the South-West Monsoon - a frequently tested exception to the general Indian monsoon pattern.

items: Puducherry UT = FOUR non-contiguous enclaves: Puducherry (in Tamil Nadu), Karaikal (in Tamil Nadu), Mahe (in Kerala), Yanam (in Andhra Pradesh).
Mahe is the UT's only west-coast (Arabian Sea) region; Puducherry, Karaikal and Yanam are all on the east coast (Bay of Bengal).
Total area approx 490 sq km; coastline approx 45 km; 4 districts (one per region); capital: Puducherry town.
Flat coastal plain terrain throughout; no hills/mountains.
Rainfall pattern follows Tamil Nadu's: North-East Monsoon (Oct-Dec) is the primary rainy season, not the South-West Monsoon.
